title: Angle, Angular Velocity and Angular Acceleration
short: Measure turning in radians: ω = Δθ/Δt and α = Δω/Δt.
trouble: Students mix degrees, revolutions and radians in one calculation.

blocks.html: Everything you learned about motion along a line has a twin for things that turn: wheels, fans, planets, a door. The turning versions use angles instead of distances, and the angle unit that makes everything work is the radian, which you met with arc length.

A radian measures an angle by the arc it cuts: $\theta = \dfrac{s}{r}$, arc length over radius. A full circle has arc $2\pi r$, so a full turn is $\dfrac{2\pi r}{r} = 2\pi$ rad. Because $\theta$ is a ratio of two lengths, the radian has no real unit, and that is exactly why formulas such as $s = r\theta$ and $v = r\omega$ work with no conversion factor, but only when the angle is in radians.

Angular position $\theta$ in radians ($1\ \text{rev} = 2\pi\ \text{rad} = 360^\circ$). Angular velocity $\role{angvel}{\omega} = \dfrac{\role[change in angle]{angle}{\Delta\theta}}{\role[time interval]{time}{\Delta t}}$ in rad/s. Angular acceleration $\role{angacc}{\alpha} = \dfrac{\role[change in angular velocity]{angvel}{\Delta\omega}}{\role[time interval]{time}{\Delta t}}$ in rad/s². Counterclockwise is usually positive, and $\alpha$ against the turning means slowing down.

blocks.title: Revolutions per minute to rad/s
blocks.q: A record turns at $45$ rpm (revolutions per minute). Find $\omega$ in rad/s.
steps: Each revolution is $2\pi$ rad, and each minute is $60\ \text{s}$.

blocks.title: Slowing down
blocks.q: A ceiling fan at $180$ rpm is switched off and stops in $12\ \text{s}$. Find its average angular acceleration, taking its direction of turning as positive.
steps: Negative: the angular acceleration points against the turning, so the fan slows.

blocks.title: Arc length
blocks.q: A point $0.30\ \text{m}$ from a wheel's axle turns through $120^\circ$. How far does it travel?

blocks.html: Mixing degrees, revolutions and radians in one calculation. Putting $120$ (degrees) into $s = r\theta$ gives an arc of $36\ \text{m}$ for a $0.30\ \text{m}$ wheel, far more than its whole circumference ($1.9\ \text{m}$). Convert every angle to radians before using $s = r\theta$ or $v = r\omega$, and check that an arc for less than one turn is less than $2\pi r$.
